title: Building an Internal Developer Platform with Artificial Intelligence
gist: At KubeCon Europe, Whitney Lee and Viktor Farcic argued that AI agents are replacing portals like Backstage as the internal developer platform interface, with semantic search over Git, Slack, Jira and meeting transcripts supplying context, guardrails governing what executes, and OpenTelemetry traces serving as the only evidence, test data and audit trail for non-deterministic agent behaviour.

themes.theme: Agents as the next platform interface

insights.claim: Agents are the next revolution of platforms: where developer tooling used to mean Backstage, it now means agents.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Portal-based IDP vendors face substitution risk from conversational agent interfaces.
insights.quote: Agents are the next revolution of platforms. You want to give your developers tooling to do stuff; before it was Backstage, now it’s agents

insights.claim: An agent works by taking developer input, combining it with system context and sending it to a model, which either answers or executes a tool selected from descriptions of what each tool can do.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Tool descriptions, not model choice, are the control surface platform teams actually own.

insights.claim: Companies are building their own agents specifically to make things secure, with guardrails that block or allow certain actions, distinguishing what can execute automatically from what requires specific approval.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The build-versus-buy decision for agent platforms is being driven by security policy rather than capability.

insights.claim: With an LLM the input can be anything a user provides and the output is whatever the model thinks it should do, so the platform team cannot limit what will happen at the model layer.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Because the model layer is unbounded, enforcement has to live at the tool and guardrail layer, which is where platform investment should go.
insights.quote: We have no idea what the input or output is

insights.claim: The talk was presented at KubeCon & CloudNativeCon Europe under the title AI Meets Internal Developer Platform, situating agentic IDPs inside the cloud-native mainstream rather than as an experiment.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Cloud-native conference programming is a leading indicator of where platform engineering budgets move next.

themes.theme: Semantic search quality is a data problem, not a model problem

insights.claim: The quality of semantic search is not defined by the embedding model or the vector database, which are commodities, but by what you put in and how you slice it.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: If embeddings and vector stores are commodities, vendor value accrues to ingestion, chunking and freshness, not to the database layer.
insights.quote: The quality of semantic search is not defined by the embedding model or the vector database. Those are commodities. It’s defined by what you put in and how you slice it.

insights.claim: The first mistake is assuming documentation is the source; it is one source and usually the worst one because it is outdated.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Knowledge-retrieval projects that start with the docs wiki are starting from the weakest corpus.
insights.quote: It’s *one* source, and usually the worst one, because it’s outdated.

insights.claim: The real sources of institutional knowledge are Git repositories with manifests and code, pull request discussions, Slack threads explaining why a database was rejected, Jira tickets, wiki pages and Zoom transcripts of design meetings, because that is where 'how we like to do things' lives.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Agent context pipelines create a new integration market across collaboration tools, and the tools holding the richest tacit knowledge gain strategic value.
insights.quote: That’s where "how we like to do things" lives.

insights.claim: Embedding a forty-page document as a single vector yields one blob that is vaguely about everything and precisely about nothing; chunks must stand on their own as a section, function or resource definition and carry metadata for repo, team and date.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Chunking strategy and metadata are the concrete implementation details that decide whether an internal agent is useful.
insights.quote: If you embed a forty-page document as a single vector, you get one blob that is vaguely about everything and precisely about nothing.

insights.claim: An index is not a one-time migration: ingestion has to be continuous and deletions have to propagate, because a six-month-old index makes the agent confidently give six-month-old answers, which is worse than no answer because you trust it.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Stale retrieval is more dangerous than retrieval failure, which argues for investing in continuous ingestion infrastructure over one-off indexing projects.
insights.quote: If the information is six months old, the agent will confidently give you six-month-old answers, and that is worse than no answer, because you trust it.

insights.claim: Semantic search is for knowledge, not state: the current state of a cluster changes every second and should be fetched live through a tool rather than embedded.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The knowledge-versus-state split is a reusable architectural rule that prevents a large class of agent hallucination.
insights.quote: The current state of your cluster is not knowledge; it’s state, and it changes every second. Don’t embed it — give the agent a tool to fetch it live.

insights.claim: When an agent's answer is wrong, the retrieval is usually the culprit rather than the LLM, and traces showing which chunks came back for a given question are how you diagnose it.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Debugging effort and vendor spend should be directed at the retrieval layer rather than at swapping models.
insights.quote: When the answer is wrong, the retrieval is usually the culprit, not the LLM.

insights.claim: Vector search lets a user, or more likely their coding agent, retrieve information across tools without knowing where it lives or guessing the exact words, because indexing is by semantic similarity.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The primary consumer of internal search is shifting from humans to coding agents, which changes what the interface must optimise for.

themes.theme: Traces as the only evidence for non-deterministic systems

insights.claim: With a normal application you re-run it with the same input and watch it break again, but asking an agent the same question twice produces two different execution paths, so the trace is not a debugging convenience, it is the only evidence the thing ever happened the way it did.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Non-determinism destroys reproduction-based debugging, making trace capture mandatory infrastructure rather than optional observability.
insights.quote: Ask the same question twice, and you get two different execution paths.

insights.claim: Agent traces show which models an agent uses, which tools it chooses, what those calls cost in tokens, and the path it takes to accomplish a task.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Token cost attribution per tool call is the foundation of any agentic FinOps practice.

insights.claim: Traces let you see the request go from user to agent to tools and are probably the only way to understand what happened after it happened.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Post-hoc reconstruction is the only available mode of analysis for agent incidents.
insights.quote: Traces allow you to see the request going from the user to the agent to the tools. They are probably the only way to understand what is happening after it happened.

insights.claim: A tool that never gets called, or always gets called wrongly, is a tool description problem, not a model problem.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Fixing agent behaviour is often a documentation-editing task, which is far cheaper than model fine-tuning or replacement.
insights.quote: A tool that never gets called, or always gets called wrongly, is a tool description problem, not a model problem.

insights.claim: One badly scoped semantic search can drag fifty thousand tokens into the context and you will only ever see that in a trace.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Unobserved context bloat is a direct and hidden line item on agentic inference bills.
insights.quote: one badly scoped semantic search can drag fifty thousand tokens into the context and you will only ever see that in a trace

insights.claim: If an agent changes something in production, somebody will eventually ask who approved it, and 'the AI did it' is not an acceptable answer, making the audit trail the third thing to inspect in every trace.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Agent audit trails are a compliance requirement waiting to be formalised, which creates a product category for governance tooling.
insights.quote: "the AI did it" is not an acceptable answer

insights.claim: Real traces are the best test data: the questions developers actually ask and the paths the agent actually took make a far better evaluation set than anything invented in a meeting.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Production telemetry becomes the eval corpus, giving incumbents with live agent traffic a compounding data advantage.
insights.quote: Real traces are your test data.

themes.theme: Observability tooling and the platform feedback loop

insights.claim: OpenTelemetry has semantic conventions for GenAI, with spans for model calls carrying the model name, token counts, tool invocations and their arguments.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A vendor-neutral standard for agent telemetry already exists, which limits lock-in from proprietary LLM observability tools.

insights.claim: With OpenTelemetry the data can be sent anywhere, including Jaeger or Grafana Tempo for traces, Prometheus for metrics and Loki for logs, while commercial platforms Datadog, Honeycomb, Dynatrace and Elastic all ingest OpenTelemetry as well.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Agent observability flows into the existing observability vendor landscape rather than creating a separate one, which favours incumbents.
insights.quote: With OpenTelemetry you can send the data anywhere: Jaeger or Grafana Tempo for traces, Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs.

insights.claim: At scale, agent observability becomes platform discovery: traces tell the platform team what developers are actually trying to accomplish through the platform.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Agent telemetry replaces surveys and roadmap guesswork as the primary source of internal platform product requirements.
insights.quote: With agent traces at scale, agent observability becomes platform discovery.

insights.claim: A feedback loop forms in which developers interact with the agent, traces show how the agent and platform responded, and together they show the platform team where developer experience can improve.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Platform teams gain a continuous measurement loop, shortening the cycle between developer friction and platform investment.

insights.claim: A single trace tells you what one agent did for debugging purposes, while thousands of traces tell you how developers are using your platform, two distinct uses of the same telemetry.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The same data asset serves both incident response and product strategy, which improves the ROI case for trace retention.
insights.quote: A single trace can tell you what an agent did, which helps with debugging. Looking at thousands of traces can tell you how developers are using your platform.
